lesson.title: Python Functions
lesson.description: Design functions with explicit inputs, useful return values, predictable scope, and maintainable signatures.
learning_objectives: Trace arguments, local names and return values
Use positional, keyword, variadic and default arguments safely
Avoid mutable-default and accidental caller-mutation bugs
Implement and test a fully specified pure normalization function

sections.title: Calls, parameters and returned values
sections.learning_objective: Trace arguments, local names and return values
sections.markdown: A function groups instructions behind a name. In def cost(price, quantity=1), price and quantity are parameters. cost(4, 3) supplies arguments 4 and 3. Python binds local parameter names, executes the body, and sends the expression after return back to the caller. print displays text; it does not return that text. Reaching the end without return produces None.

examples.code:
def cost(price, quantity=1):
    return price * quantity
print(cost(4, 3))
print(cost(quantity=2, price=5))

sections.title: Local names and shared mutable objects
sections.learning_objective: Use positional, keyword, variadic and default arguments safely
sections.markdown: A parameter is a local name referring to the supplied object. Rebinding that name changes the local reference. Mutating a shared list changes the object the caller also sees. A pure helper reads inputs and returns a result without altering caller-owned objects. Use a new list when the contract promises no mutation.

examples.code:
def extended(values, extra):
    return values + [extra]
original = [2, 4]
print(extended(original, 6))
print(original)

sections.title: Defaults, keyword arguments, *args and **kwargs
sections.learning_objective: Avoid mutable-default and accidental caller-mutation bugs
sections.markdown: Defaults make selected arguments optional. Keyword arguments state parameter names explicitly. A star before a parameter collects remaining positional arguments into a tuple; two stars collect remaining keyword arguments into a dictionary. The function below sums positional amounts and obtains an optional adjustment from named options. Unknown or conflicting arguments should have an explicit API policy in real code.

sections.title: A new list for each call
sections.learning_objective: Implement and test a fully specified pure normalization function
sections.markdown: A default expression is evaluated when def executes, not for every later call. A default list can therefore be shared across calls. Use None as a sentinel and allocate a fresh list inside the function when an omitted argument means a fresh collection. This example makes two independent lists; supplying an existing list deliberately allows mutation and should be documented.

examples.code:
def append_item(item, values=None):
    if values is None:
        values = []
    values.append(item)
    return values
print(append_item('a'))
print(append_item('b'))

sections.title: Worked solution: nonnegative score normalization
sections.learning_objective: Implement and test a fully specified pure normalization function
sections.markdown: Contract: scores is a finite list of nonnegative finite numbers. Return a new list; do not mutate scores. Return [] for an empty list. If the maximum is zero, return zeros of the same length; otherwise divide every score by that maximum. Reject negative values with ValueError. First check the domain, then the empty boundary, then find the maximum, then handle zero before division. For [2, 4], the maximum is 4 and the result is [0.5, 1.0]. The algorithm uses O(n) time and O(n) output space. Finite-number validation is an input precondition for this introductory contract, not silently implemented by type hints.

examples.code:
def normalized_scores(scores):
    if any(value < 0 for value in scores):
        raise ValueError("scores must be nonnegative")
    if not scores:
        return []
    maximum = max(scores)
    if maximum == 0:
        return [0 for value in scores]
    return [value / maximum for value in scores]
values = [2, 4]
print(normalized_scores(values))
print(values)
print(normalized_scores([]))
print(normalized_scores([0, 0]))

sections.title: Revision and independent practice
sections.learning_objective: Implement and test a fully specified pure normalization function
sections.markdown: Trace a new call before running it. Check return versus print, the binding of positional and keyword arguments, and whether a list is shared. For normalization, test an empty list, all zeros, unequal positive values, a negative value and unchanged caller input. Writing a reflection or reading this lesson never awards mastery. Scored coding requires a reviewed contract in an approved assessment pool; ordinary legacy Arena is not a clean-transfer shortcut.

summary: Parameters are local names; arguments supply objects.
return sends a value; print displays text.
Defaults are created at definition time.
A pure function preserves caller-owned state and follows a complete boundary contract.
interview_takeaways: Trace a call with exact values.
Explain shared mutation and default lifetimes.
Support a claimed contract with boundary tests.
common_mistakes: Mutating an input despite a pure-function contract
Dividing by a zero maximum or calling max on an empty list

exercises.title: Trace: x=10; def double(x): return x*2
exercises.prompt_markdown: Trace: x=10; def double(x): return x*2. Explain double(3) and the outer x afterwards.
hints: Write down inputs, the function body, its return value, and one boundary case.

content.reference_answer: double(3) returns 6. Its local parameter x refers to 3. The outer x remains 10 because the call does not assign to the outer name.

exercises.title: Fix def square(n): print(n*n) so callers can use square(4)+1
exercises.prompt_markdown: Fix def square(n): print(n*n) so callers can use square(4)+1. State the final value.
hints: Write down inputs, the function body, its return value, and one boundary case.

content.reference_answer: Use def square(n): return n*n. square(4) returns 16, so square(4)+1 is 17. Printing alone returns None, which cannot be added to 1.

exercises.title: Implement normalized_scores using the full nonnegative finite-list contract in the worked
exercises.prompt_markdown: Implement normalized_scores using the full nonnegative finite-list contract in the worked section. Include empty, zero, negative and no-mutation tests.
hints: Write down inputs, the function body, its return value, and one boundary case.

content.reference_answer:
def normalized_scores(scores):
    if any(value < 0 for value in scores):
        raise ValueError("scores must be nonnegative")
    if not scores:
        return []
    maximum = max(scores)
    if maximum == 0:
        return [0 for value in scores]
    return [value / maximum for value in scores]
values = [2, 4]
print(normalized_scores(values))
print(values)
print(normalized_scores([]))
print(normalized_scores([0, 0]))
Expected printed output:
[0.5, 1.0]
[2, 4]
[]
[0, 0]
A call with [-1] must raise ValueError. Finite numbers are an explicit precondition.
rubric: Returns a new list without input mutation

exercises.title: Explain why items=[] is unsafe when an omitted argument should create a fresh list
exercises.prompt_markdown: Explain why items=[] is unsafe when an omitted argument should create a fresh list. Give the repair.
hints: Write down inputs, the function body, its return value, and one boundary case.

content.reference_answer: The default list is constructed once when def executes, then reused. Use items=None and inside the body if items is None: items=[] before appending. Two omitted-argument calls then receive independent lists.
